work.title: The Analects
work.notes: The Analects is a received collection of sayings and dialogues compiled by disciples and later followers, not a book written by Confucius. Preserve speaker attribution and canonical book/chapter references.

edition.label: James Legge English translation from The Chinese Classics; Project Gutenberg #3330
edition.licenseNote: Project Gutenberg metadata states public domain in the USA; verify the law of the deployment jurisdiction before production redistribution. This is a historical translation whose Victorian terminology should not silently replace the classical Chinese concepts.

passages.citationLabel: The Analects 1.1, Legge trans., Project Gutenberg #3330
passages.translationText: The Master said, 'Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? 2. 'Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?' 3. 'Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?'
passages.interpretiveNote: Legge presents learning as sustained practice, fellowship, and composure when unrecognized. His phrase “complete virtue” is historical translation language and should be checked against 君子 rather than treated as a transparent equivalent.
passages.period: Analects textual tradition; historical English translation

passages.citationLabel: The Analects 2.3, Legge trans., Project Gutenberg #3330
passages.translationText: The Master said, 'If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. 2. 'If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.'
passages.interpretiveNote: The historical translation contrasts external compliance under punishment with cultivated shame and willing order under virtue and ritual. It does not establish that institutions and laws are unnecessary.
passages.period: Analects textual tradition; historical English translation

passages.locator: Book VI, Chapter XXVIII in this edition; commonly Analects 6.30; OEBPS/4804000333999934205_3330-0.txt.xhtml
passages.citationLabel: The Analects 6.30, Legge trans., Project Gutenberg #3330
passages.translationText: Now the man of perfect virtue, wishing to be established himself, seeks also to establish others; wishing to be enlarged himself, he seeks also to enlarge others.
passages.interpretiveNote: Legge's “perfect virtue” translates 仁 in this context. The passage connects one's own cultivation with enabling others, while the Chinese 立 and 達 carry nuances not exhausted by “established” and “enlarged.”
passages.period: Analects textual tradition; historical English translation

passages.citationLabel: The Analects 7.8, Legge trans., Project Gutenberg #3330
passages.translationText: The Master said, 'I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, nor help out any one who is not anxious to explain himself. When I have presented one corner of a subject to any one, and he cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson.'
passages.interpretiveNote: This is an early statement of responsive, inquiry-driven teaching. The wording should not be used to deny assistance; the focus is the learner's active participation and capacity to extend a prompt.
passages.period: Analects textual tradition; historical English translation

passages.citationLabel: The Analects 12.2, Legge trans., Project Gutenberg #3330
passages.translationText: Chung-kung asked about perfect virtue. The Master said, 'It is, when you go abroad, to behave to every one as if you were receiving a great guest; to employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice; not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself; to have no murmuring against you in the country, and none in the family.' Chung-kung said, 'Though I am deficient in intelligence and vigour, I will make it my business to practise this lesson.'
passages.interpretiveNote: This historical translation combines reverent conduct with reciprocity. “Perfect virtue” and “rules of propriety” are Legge's period vocabulary and should be related back to 仁 and 禮.
passages.period: Analects textual tradition; historical English translation
